noticias.titulo: Crimea bridge shut after reported Ukrainian strike, as Russia hits Kyiv crossings
noticias.resumen: The bridge linking Crimea and Russia has reportedly sustained major damage, while two routes through Kyiv are closed.
noticias.texto:
Crimea bridge shut after reported Ukrainian strike, as Russia hits Kyiv crossings
- Published
A key bridge linking occupied Crimea and Russia is closed after reports a Ukrainian strike inflicted major damage, during a night in which the warring countries both targeted major crossings.
A former adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky shared images purporting to show that a section of the Crimea bridge - also known as the Kerch Bridge - had collapsed into the water.
Meanwhile, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges, important routes over the Dnipro River, were closed after Russian ballistic missile strikes.
Those attacks came a day after Ukraine began its most recent attempt to disable the Crimea bridge, a prized Kremlin asset seen as a symbol of Russia's occupation.
Two people were killed in that strike overnight on Sunday, the Russian-installed governor of Crimea said.
Former Ukrainian adviser Anton Gerashchenko shared images and video footage appearing to show extensive damage to the bridge from the latest strike, with a support arch and road section seen protruding from the water below. BBC News has not independently verified those images.
The bridge, which has come under repeated attack by Ukrainian forces, was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2018.
While Ukraine has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the Crimea bridge is an attempt do increase the political cost on Putin.
The severity of the latest strike on the route, which is protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences, is still not fully clear - but Russian state media reported a meeting was due to be held on Tuesday to discuss the situation.
Crimea's Moscow-backed governor Sergei Aksyonov confirmed on Telegram that traffic over the bridge had been suspended.
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between the Chinese, US and Russian leaders in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.
Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems".
"Some areas are experiencing disruptions to water and heating supplies", he added.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services were damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Residents of Kyiv typically shelter in the city's underground stations during air raids.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
These latest Russian strikes will cause major disruption, with traffic already reportedly building in the capital.
Several of the capital's major bridges were also targeted by Russian drone strikes in October.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkast region, according to local officials.
Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said.
The latest round of tit-for-tat strikes came after US, Ukrainian and European officials held talks on ways to facilitate "direct engagement" between Russia and Europe to end the war.
Following Monday's meeting, US envoy Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, said the US was committed to providing Ukraine with a "strong, credible security guarantees", as well as a path towards EU membership.
He added that Nato "will remain a critical pillar of European security", and that preparations are underway for a further multilateral meeting "in the near future".
Zelensky said that the meeting was "difficult", adding that more needed to be done to support Ukraine's defence against Russian ballistic missile strikes.
The Ukrainian president has long called for European nations to be included in any peace talks, which he argues is necessary because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the EU.
He also used his address to say Moscow is receiving "dozens of missiles per month" from North Korea.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian officials said that the final death toll from a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian village of Kamyshuvakha earlier this month had reached 72.
Four people are still considered missing after the bombing, which Ukrainian officials say is one of the deadliest individual attacks since the start of the war in 2022.
Footage, from a camera on one of the killed police officers, showed residents going to an underground shelter after the initial attack on 2 November. Soon after a blast is heard and flames are seen as the shelter is hit.
Ukrainian police said of those killed were police officers, "staff of the gymnasium, utility workers and medical personnel".
Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

noticias.titulo: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72
noticias.resumen: Efforts to recover bodies after a “double-tap” attack in southern Ukraine are being hampered by continuing Russian strikes, officials say.
noticias.texto:
Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72
- Published
Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.
Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.
Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site.
The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there have been multiple Russian strikes during the rescue.
The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged.
"Due to the threat of repeated shelling, emergency workers are constantly forced to periodically suspend work and retreat to a safe place," it added.
The DSNS said the death toll had risen to at least 72 people making it one of the deadliest single incidents since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Oleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, said rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".
He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.
BBC Verify has confirmed videos being shared by Ukrainian police that show rescue workers at the scene shouting "drone, drone" and running for cover on the day after the 2 November attack. A group can also be seen treating a victim.
Bodies are still to be recovered from the rubble, Oleksiy said. "The enemy knows perfectly well that what is being carried out there is essentially a humanitarian operation to search for the dead."
BBC Verify has asked the Russian Ministry of Defence for comment specifically about the Komyshuvakha attacks but has not received a response.
A general statement released on 2 November by the Russian MoD said it had targeted energy and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian military across the country.
While there are no military or industrial facilities in Komyshuvakha it is close to a key route used for Ukrainian troop movements, supplies and evacuations. The village was previously reported to have been struck by the Russians on 28 October.
Fears of second strike heard on police radios
Local people headed to the shelter area on 2 November after being told by a local Telegram group that aid would be distributed between 10:00 and 12:00 local time (08:00-10:00 GMT). Ukrainian authorities said an initial strike, at 09:45 local time, hit buildings above ground killing one woman.
Bodycam footage, released by Ukrainian police in edited segments and analysed by BBC Verify, shows people trying to free a casualty from the rubble before declaring she had died.
Throughout the footage, warnings of an impending second strike can be heard on police radios with increasing urgency until people are instructed to run to the underground shelter.
The same footage, which was taken around an hour after the first attack, goes on to show people in a shelter. As they wait in silence a large explosion can be heard and the video goes dark.
Aftermath video filmed later shows bodies being recovered from a large crater immediately above the shelter. Twisted iron and rubble from the structure below can be seen beneath the surface.
Funerals have been held almost daily for the victims of the attack, including locals working to administer aid distribution, those seeking to collect it and soldiers who officials say arrived to assist with rescue efforts.
Trevor Ball, bomb disposal expert at intelligence firm at Armament Research Services, said a crater seen in the footage was consistent with the damage and depth left by a FAB-3000, a 3,000kg Russian bomb which can destroy underground structures.
His comments were echoed by Chris Proops, an ex-UK National Crime Agency investigator, who said the scale of the damage at the scene matched the size of the FAB-3000.
Ball and Proops both confirmed verified photos of munition fragments obtained by BBC Verify from Ukrainian authorities show part of a guidance kit that is compatible with the FAB-3000, which increases the weapon's accuracy and allows it to be fired from a greater distance from the target.
International law experts told BBC Verify that Russia had committed a war crime if it knowingly attacked rescue workers.
Ben Saul, professor of international law at the University of Sydney, said this "appears to be either a deliberate attack on civilians or civilian objects - a war crime - or an indiscriminate attack - also a war crime".
Prof Samuel Moyn of Yale University said "directly targeting rescuers or their equipment is a gross violation of international humanitarian law". Precautions have to be taken to ensure that strikes target combatants rather than others, he added.
Additional reporting by Margaryta Maliukova, BBC Monitoring

noticias.titulo: Imran Khan seeks urgent medical care fearing he 'may not return alive'
noticias.resumen: Pakistan's ex-prime minister, who has been in prison since August 2023, says he has been denied justice.
noticias.texto:
Imran Khan seeks urgent medical care fearing he 'may not return alive'
- Published
Pakistan's jailed former PM Imran Khan has appealed for urgent medical treatment, saying that his and his wife's health has been deteriorating.
"At 74, this unrelenting state is taking me to a place from which I may not return alive," the cricket star-turned-politician wrote in a letter published by his lawyer Salman Safdar.
Authorities in Islamabad maintain that Khan gets seen weekly by doctors, who have assessed that he is of "satisfactory" health.
Khan, who faces more than 100 charges, has been in prison since August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year. Khan argues the cases against them, ranging from corruption to selling state gifts, are politically motivated.
Concerns over Khan's health have grown louder in the past year, with his family claiming he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.
In his letter, Khan wrote that doctors have told him he is "highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest", and that his heart has already "suffered damage".
He also expressed concern for Bushra Bibi, whom he says suffered a detached retina in April and underwent surgery in secrecy. Khan said he fears she may lose her sight without further surgery.
"I have fought impossible legal battles in countless cases, and I have not stopped. But the system has stopped giving me justice," he wrote.
He said that he is being held in solitary confinement for up to 22 hours a day, where he is allowed neither visits by his family nor access to books and television, and that this has "taken a heavy toll" on his mental health.
He also claimed he had only seen his lawyers four times over the past year.
"I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," he wrote.
Pakistan's parliamentary affairs minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry disputed these claims, saying Khan is "provided with all facilities in prison, including food of his own choosing".
"[He] is currently the most well-accommodated prisoner in Pakistan," the minister told reporters.
Authorities also say Khan was taken to a government-run hospital for an eye injection a week ago, where doctors deemed him "clinically stable".
Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.
His arrest in May 2023 sparked large-scale, violent protests by supporters, who ransacked the corps commander's residence in Lahore, smashing chandeliers and making away with furniture, paintings, and even peacocks, among other things.
At least eight people died in the protests and the army were called in to quell the violence.
Even behind bars, Khan remains a force in Pakistani politics.
Thousands of his supporters took to the streets in early October in a dayslong march, demanding his release. Authorities later ordered a crackdown on protests and imposed a state of emergency in Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Former international cricket captains have made several appeals in recent months to Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, insisting that Khan be given proper medical care.

noticias.titulo: OpenAI sued by California over Hugging Face attack
noticias.resumen: Attorney General Rob Bonta alleges that the artificial intelligence misled and endangered the public.
noticias.texto:
OpenAI sued by California over Hugging Face attack
- Published
California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the ChatGPT-maker misled and endangered the public by developing artificial intelligence (AI) models without proper safeguards.
In the lawsuit, Bonta cited the July 2026 attack on the AI platform Hugging Face by experimental OpenAI agents which accessed the internet to breach that company's internal systems.
Bonta claimed OpenAI created a public nuisance and violated the state's unfair competition laws.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the BBC in a statement that Bonta's lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab".
Other major AI developers including Anthropic, Meta, and Google have also said their models have staged similar attacks.
But Bonta's lawsuit, filed in San Francisco, where the company is headquartered, appears to be the first such suit filed by a US state.
Hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated the Hugging Face attack over two days even though they were supposed to be contained in a safe testing environment.
The incident drew added scrutiny because the agents went as far as attempting to cover their tracks.
Bonta announced an investigation into the incident in September, and served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of its probe.
"The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it - this disregard for public safety violated California law," Bonta said in a statement on Monday.
OpenAI said it has been transparent and responsive to the Attorney General's office.
"We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged - and will continue to engage - constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," the company said.
The company added that, since the Hugging Face incident, it has worked to understand and address "misaligned model activity" which industry figures often refer to as rogue agents.
Nathan Calvin, chief strategy officer at AI safety campaign group Encode AI, said the lawsuit "recognises something we at Encode have long raised alarms about".
"OpenAI and other companies developing frontier AI systems have safety and security practices that are insufficient to protect the public from risks that could be catastrophic," he said.

noticias.titulo: Vance says he will decide 'sometime next year' about 2028 US presidential run
noticias.resumen: The US vice-president tells Fox News that when he makes a decision to run or otherwise, he will "be all in on whatever that decision is".
noticias.texto:
Vance says he will decide 'sometime next year' about 2028 US presidential run
- Published
US Vice-President JD Vance has said he will make a decision "sometime next year" about whether or not he will run for president in 2028.
In an interview with Fox News, Vance would not provide a timeline on making a determination, but signaled he is not in a hurry to make up his mind.
"I haven't made a decision. We'll figure it out sometime next year," Vance said. When pressed by host Laura Ingraham, he added: "When I make a decision, I'll be all in on whatever that decision is."
The comments came amid growing interest in Vance's next moves in the weeks since voters handed both President Donald Trump and Republicans a resounding defeat in the midterm elections.
People in Vance's orbit who have spoken to the BBC said the November elections did not change the timeline around his decision-making process for 2028. He is expected to run but allies believe he could wait several months to make a final decision.
Speculation about Vance's White House aspirations began the moment President Trump selected him as his 2024 running mate. The pick positioned Vance, who entered the White House as one of the youngest vice-presidents in US history, as the most likely heir to Trump's Make America Great Again (Maga) movement.
But while serving in office, Vance has carefully avoided discussing his own political ambitions.
He kept that up during the midterms, when supporters frequently interrupted his campaign speeches to urge him to run in 2028. Vance's stock response was that Republicans needed to focus on the election at hand in November.
But with the midterms in the rearview mirror, and Republicans eager to move on from their 2026 drubbing, the next election at hand is now the 2028 presidential race.
- Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war 
  - Published5 November
- The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now? 
  - Published8 November
Vance would likely jump to the top of the Republican primary field whenever he launches his bid, should he choose to run. But the contest is expected to be a competitive process with a large field of candidates.
Numerous other high-profile Republicans are rumoured to be interested in running or have said publicly that they are mulling a White House bid.
The list includes Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, outgoing Florida Governor and 2024 hopeful Ron DeSantis, and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, among others.
Trump has praised Vance and Rubio on several occasions, while also insisting that he is not sure who he will endorse in 2028 - or if he will weigh in at all.
The president's endorsement would be influential with the Maga base. But the midterms revealed widespread frustration with many of his second-term policies, complicating the path forward for potential candidates like Vance who are tied to Trump's agenda.
Vance blamed the midterm results on the war with Iran in a post-election social media post. In it, he also mapped out a plan for winning back Republican voters, which included ending the war and focusing on the economy.
The message was widely seen as a first step by Vance to distance himself from Trump ahead of a 2028 run.
In the Fox News interview, Vance reiterated his view that the war came with a "political cost", but said it has not damaged his relationship with Trump.
"There's no daylight" on the Iran war between Trump and senior administration officials including himself, Vance said.
He added that Trump would not let the conflict become a "forever war" and said the administration would not let the war, which was launched by the US and Israel in February 2026, even become "a two-year commitment".
Vance also discussed the nationwide air traffic outrage last week, which brought air travel across the US to a standstill for several hours. The vice-president called on lawmakers to fix the issue in the final weeks of the current congressional session.
He also touched on the scandal engulfing Nvidia, its former CEO Jensen Huang and its implications for US-China relations. Vance said there was still no "clarity" about the accuracy of reports that a woman with whom Huang reportedly had an affair with was indeed a Chinese spy.
"There is a lack of clarity about it. I don't know and [Trump] doesn't know whether this woman was a spy or not," Vance said.

noticias.titulo: Pope Leo hit by flying rosary while waving to crowds in Peru
noticias.resumen: The pontiff was struck in the face by what is thought to be prayer beads while travelling aboard the popemobile to deliver a farewell Mass.
noticias.texto:
Pope Leo hit by flying rosary while waving to crowds in Peru
Pope Leo XIV was struck in the face by what is thought to be rosary prayer beads while travelling in the popemobile to deliver a farewell Mass in Peru.
Photos and video show the pope rubbing his eye shortly after the object was tossed toward him. He sustained no injuries and the Mass went ahead.

noticias.titulo: China is hosting the world's leaders in its AI wonderland. Here's what they won't see
noticias.resumen: Leave Shenzhen's tech-flecked city skyline and you run into the challenges confronting Xi's China.
noticias.texto:
China is hosting the world's leaders in its AI wonderland. Here's what they won't see
- Published
At 27, Huang Shihua is living the Chinese Dream.
He works as an engineer for a leading humanoid robot company in Shenzhen. The sprawling south-eastern metropolis is touted by China as the origin story for a high-tech future powered by artificial intelligence, robotics and home-grown innovation.
Drones soar across the sky to deliver your dinner, driverless taxis play relaxing music as you journey to your destination, and robots don't just hand you a cappuccino - they explain the origin of your coffee beans.
"We have created a miracle in Shenzhen," Huang says, surrounded by humanoid robots making coffee and playing chess. "Many young people from across China, full of passion and dreams, have flocked here."
Now they all spend their days figuring out ways to make robots smarter.
The Chinese call Shenzhen the "city of dreams". The moniker suits it: one of China's wealthiest, it is close to Hong Kong and the place where the country's explosive growth took off decades ago.
Its manufacturing inventory mirrors China's rise: cabbage patch dolls, then TVs, later iPhones, electric vehicles, drones and now the robots, which are drawing Huang and a new generation of Chinese ambition.
The "miracles" these young engineers are chasing are central to Xi Jinping's bold vision for China. So where better to show it off than Shenzhen, which will be centre-stage when US President Donald Trump, Russian leader Vladimir Putin and others arrive for a global economic summit this week.
And yet there is another side to this flashy, coastal city, a side that they will not get to see. Drive away from towering skyscrapers towards Shajing and Songgang, once the source of much of the world's electronics, and you will run into the challenges confronting Xi's China.
"Everyone feels life is hard," one construction worker tells us. "Lots of factories have relocated and workers lost their jobs."
China remains exceptionally good at making things - and Shenzhen is proof of that. But the city also holds the evidence for what ails the world's second-largest economy. The property crisis is not over, denting confidence in the future. This is one of China's most expensive cities but even here, our taxi driver tells us, his house is now only worth a third of its original price.
A weak property market and sluggish consumer spending mean many households are buying less. Factories are increasingly relying on exports while many manufacturers have cut production, downsized, automated or moved elsewhere in search of cheaper labour.
The result is a growing number of workers turning to temporary jobs in the gig economy, often with lower pay and fewer benefits.
"Shenzhen is not a magic place," says one delivery driver in his 40s, unwilling to give his name.
"Some say there is gold everywhere in Shenzhen, but it's not like that anymore. It's not a city where you can come and thrive. If you don't work hard, you won't have anything."
The BBC spent several days in Shenzhen exploring these two very different sides of China's progress: on the one hand is the dazzling promise of AI, and on the other are the anxieties of workers who worry if there will be room for them in the future it creates.
Wednesday is sandwich and bubble tea day in the offices of DexForce Technologies.
The elevator is packed with young engineers and developers headed to the right floor for the free carbs and sugar that will fuel their afternoon. They jostle past their creations en route: human-sized, yellow robots whose limbs fill every available corner.
"I believe that in a decade, robots will be able to better serve humanity by taking on highly repetitive or even dangerous tasks," Huang says. That could be anything from serving coffee to working in mines, and they are being trained for all of that in this laboratory for the future, where machines flail, jerk or lurch into motion as they learn to behave.
To him, "Shenzhen is another 'America'. Because, much like in the US, many young people have been able to realise their dreams and earn the wealth they desire."
This is what Xi wants to hear as he pushes China to lead the world in advanced tech. Shenzhen has indeed long been a place for seeking opportunity but Huang and his colleagues want to do much more. They don't simply want to continue China's manfuacturing supremacy. They want to transform it.
Beyond making "our lives more convenient and comfortable", Huang sees AI as helping "the entire world become one family - a global village. AI has the potential to foster equality and the prospect of AI-driven equality is, to me, the most exciting possibility of all."
Smiling enthusiastically, he explains how he hopes that robots can help emerging economies across Africa and South East Asia catch up by reshaping their production lines too.
This tech-charged optimism, which is everywhere in the building, jars with the uncertainty elsewhere in Shenzhen, where robots are nowhere to be found. Yet. But that's just the first of the differences.
In Huang's side of the city, tech and finance workers stroll to the office after a morning workout, sipping coffee that probably cost more than 30 yuan ($4.50; Â£3.40).
On the other side, scooters whizz through streets piled high with goods being shuttled between factories as vendors sell whole breakfast plates of spicy noodles for under 3 yuan.
Outside one of the city's tallest skyscrapers, 50-year-old Ms Lu has a phone to her ear and a pen in her right hand while grabbing a bag with her left from a delivery driver.
She shouts four key numbers at her co-worker: instructions for another Chinese woman who is waiting to take the delivery up the elevator to someone sitting at their desk.
This is the lunchtime rush outside SEG plaza, home to 70 storeys of thousands of tenants. Lu used to be one of them. "I ran a small business on the second floor. I sold circuit boards," she says. "But it's getting so hard to do business these days and the rental fees got higher."
Often likened to China's Silicon Valley, Shenzhen has seen rents soar with the influx of new capital, squeezing out smaller, more traditional businesses. At 50, Ms Lu couldn't find another job until the delivery drivers came to her with a plan.
The wait for the elevator can take half an hour â wasted money for a driver trying to fill as many orders as possible. So Ms Lu became a new layer in the ever-evolving gig economy.
"The delivery drivers bring food here to the building entrance. We pick it up and take it upstairs. The drivers pay us 2 yuan per order," she explains, always on the move. Delivery drivers earn between four to eight yuan per order, so Ms Lu gets a decent cut of their earnings.
"The lunch peak time only lasts two or three hoursâ¦ if they use our service, they can get more orders done, and we can earn some money as well. But the market is bad. These days I only earn around 200 yuan per day."
An estimated 200 million Chinese workers, roughly 40% of the urban labour force, now depend on some form of gig work. Many delivery drivers in Shenzhen tell us they chose temporary work because there are fewer opportunities at factories than before.
"We need to adapt to the situation we find ourselves in," one driver told us, "rather than waiting for it to adapt to our needs." A group of them are waiting outside the gates of an e-cigarette factory to make industrial deliveries.
Others nod in agreement. Another driver says he has little choice: "I have two children to raise and I can't stop working. I don't have time to think about anything else."
Permanent jobs often require contributions to social security and pension, which reduces take-home pay. But gig work means more cash in hand and flexibile hours.
"Most workers prefer jobs with a fixed, shorter-term duration. It allows them the flexibility to resign and leave whenever they choose; they have no desire to become permanent employees," says job agent Li Xiaohe.
Increasingly, he puts up boards on pavements advertising temporary factory jobs that pay around 22 yuan an hour for assembling small electronics.
Although agents also appear to be in a shrinking pool, with several former shop fronts shuttered: yet another sign of the downturn in traditional manufacturing.
"Our business is perhaps not as optimistic as it once was," Li admits. "We can feel the effects of Shenzhen going through a transformation."
That transformation is hard to miss.
Drones buzz above the lush grounds of a purpose built "talent park" along the city's waterfront, dipping and darting as they deliver meals to a dedicated platform. Phones held high, tourists capture them landing with their lunch.
"This is amazing. The technology is just great. I wish we had this back at home," exclaims one Canadian tourist. Our coffee order - for a five-yuan delivery - arrives in just over 15 minutes, the drone landing seamlessly so I can pick up my order.
"I heard that many years ago, Shenzhen was a fishing village," says Anle, who is visiting from Vietnam. "Ha â no more fishing village," he laughs as he orders milk tea to be delivered by drone for him and his wife.
For all the ingenuity on display, it feels more like a demonstration of what is possible rather than a mundane reality. The deliveries, which are only possible in certain locations, stop at 20:00 local time. The driverless cars, which need a separate app to order, are also a novelty â they even offer you a massage when you are on your way.
At night, in the glow of a thousand dancing lights, the drones take on a different role. They fly above the park warning people to behave and not cause trouble.
Far from the glittering skyline, workers gather around plastic tables outside restaurants serving cheap hotpot and seafood skewers.
There are more expensive restaurants along the street, but they too have taken a hit. One owner told us business is down by more than 70% as workers are hesitant to splurge on dinner.
Many of them have spent decades here, including 58-year-old construction worker Mr Wu. He arrived in Shenzhen from Sichuan in the 1990s not long after China opened the city up to foreign businesses.
He was among millions of migrants from poorer provinces who came to work on production lines or build skyscrapers. They are still coming.
All the people we spoke to came from elsewhere. They often labour up to 14 hours a day and live in shared dormitories, sustained by the prospect of stable work and decent pay to send home to their families.
For these workers, the Covid pandemic, when Chinese manufacturing hit a record low, appears to have been the first turning point.
"After Covid, our salary dropped by at least a third," Mr Wu recalls, after which wages never fully recovered.
"I will continue to work," he adds. "As long as you keep working, you will have an income. More salary or not? It doesn't matter. As long as you keep working, you will have an income. If the economy slows down, we all slow down. If it grows, we all get better."
For all these decades, Shenzhen lived up to its bargain: work hard and your life would improve.
But now, in a city that is being redefined by automation and AI, that old promise feels less secure.
  - Published22 September
  - Published12 January 2025

noticias.titulo: Taking Korea's toughest exam from behind bars
noticias.resumen: Eleven convicts at the Mandela Boys' School will be among the thousands of young Koreans taking the country's hardest exam, the Suneung.
noticias.texto:
Taking Korea's toughest exam from behind bars
- Published
Students intently focus on maths formulas written on a board before lowering their heads and taking notes as the teacher works through a sum.
The teacher's voice and the scratch of pens fill the room.
At first glance, this could be any classroom in South Korea.
But thick metal bars cover the windows and the students are wearing blue prison uniforms and rubber shoes emblazoned with the words "Korea Correctional Service".
This is Mandela Boys' School, an education facility for young prisoners inside the Seoul Southern Correctional Institution in Guro, south-west Seoul. In South Korea, young people who are sentenced to imprisonment by a criminal court must serve their time in prison.
"The boys here have committed serious offences and received criminal sentences," Jeong Yeo-gyeong, a correctional officer in the Korea Correctional Service's social reintegration division, told the BBC.
"As well as theft, there is a high proportion of serious offences, including violence, bodily injury, sexual violence and robbery."
But by opening educational institutes like Mandela, authorities are hoping to give these young offenders a chance to better their lives after they serve out their sentences.
Opened by the justice ministry in March 2023, it allows boys who were aged 17 and under when their sentences became final to prepare for school equivalency exams as well as the Suneung - the country's notoriously difficult university entrance examination - while still serving their sentences.
Held every November, the Suneung is an infamous eight-hour marathon of back-to-back exams.
Students attempt about 200 questions across various subjects, which include Korean, maths, English, social and natural sciences, among others.
The country itself comes to a standstill - construction work halts, planes are grounded and military training gets suspended to facilitate an optimal testing environment.
A total of 551,864 people have applied to take this year's Suneung on 19 November.
Around 30 prisoners are enrolled in the Suneung preparation class at Mandela Boys' School, and 11 of them have applied to take this year's exam.
Park Soo-young (not his real name), a 17-year-old inmate, has been at the Mandela Boys' Suneung preparation class for two months and hopes to study social welfare.
He tells the BBC that he had dreams of becoming a police officer before committing the crime that landed him behind bars.
He says he could not bring himself to look properly at his mother during his trial. When he turned towards her after his sentence was announced, she was crying.
"Seeing her like that, I broke down too. I wondered how I was going to live from then on, and how I could look after my mother, who was on her own. I think I kept crying for about a week while I was in the detention centre."
Looking back on his offence, he says he feels "very ashamed that I couldn't control that impulse". If he could meet his younger self, he would tell him: "Control that impulse. If you do, everything will be different."
"I'd grab myself by the collar and shake myself as I said it."
He hopes the Suneung and university will offer him a chance to start again.
"Once I'm out, I need to cut ties with the friends and people I used to know and start a new life. I think university is the only way to do that. Going to university would let me leave the area where I used to live, move somewhere else and start something new. That's why I began studying again."
But he describes beginning Suneung preparation as "a struggle every day".
"But the teachers don't let anything slip past. They keep helping us until we understand. If I don't understand something, I put my hand up and they come over and explain it.
Sometimes, if I've missed something, I keep working at it on my own. If I still can't get it, I ask the students next to me to explain," he said.
Park's day begins at 06:30 with a morning check by prison officers. He starts memorising English vocabulary and working through Korean reading passages early in the morning.
"I learn English words whenever I can, even before breakfast. From 07:00, I work through a Korean passage, something like literature or speech. We have to come down to the classroom at 08:00, so we have another check and then come down for lessons."
During breaks, students make calls to their families or leave the classroom for scheduled visits. In the evening, they return for supervised study. Once the day's activities are over, they must go back to their cells together.
Park says he studies until 22:00 before finishing for the day. If he wants to study longer hours, he needs permission from a prison officer.
But even if gets a good result this year, Park will not be allowed to leave prison and attend university straight away. He is only due to be released in 2028, but plans to use this exam as experience and continue studying next year.
"This time, I want to experience how the Suneung works and how competitive it is. Then, next year, I'll work hard from the start so I can get in the year after that."
Some former students from Mandela Boys' School have managed to get into university, according to the justice ministry.
Others have continued their studies after leaving prison, including by enrolling in residential exam preparation academies.
The inmates are taught by a team of seven prison officers, all of whom hold teaching certificates. Each is responsible for a subject.
Visiting instructors provide classes in the humanities, arts and sport, while university student volunteers help with learning. Professional psychological counselling is also available.
Park Min-yong, who applied to work here in 2023, teaches science. And alongside Suneung lessons, he works with the students' to change their habits and behaviour.
One thing he often tells them is that they need to "learn how to become adults".
He believes that while studying in itself does not necessarily turn inmates away from a life of crime, the experience of having worked hard at something: staying with a concept that makes little sense, revisiting a wrong answer and continuing even when grades do not improve straight away, is valuable in itself.
"Studying properly means pushing yourself to your limits, and that takes considerable stamina and patience," he says.
"Whether they chose to do it or not, the experience of persevering, enduring and not giving up easily may help them to some extent when they face the difficulties of life after release."
He says the material they encounter while preparing for the Suneung also gives them new things to think about.
Korean reading passages cover literature, society, science and philosophy. Students have to consider a character's perspective, examine the evidence behind an argument and understand unfamiliar concepts. They also encounter explanations that differ from their own and have to reconsider what they think.
"They gradually learn that it's not just about their own personal view - that these concepts and relationships have been developed through a shared understanding among many people," Park said.
There are difficult moments too.
Park says students sometimes cheat in classroom tests even while he is watching.
"They cheat as if it's nothing. They give each other answers, even when I'm watching them. Some repeat it after being told off. There may be an element of doing it deliberately, but often they haven't thought it through. They don't think about the impact their actions or words could have on others."
The boys also have a strong desire for recognition, he says.
"It's all the time. 'Look how much I've done. Look how much my grades have improved. I've done this much - haven't I done well?' They're always like that. They're hungry for it."
Not everyone agrees with this initiative though.
One criticism is that young people who have not committed crimes also face fierce competition for university places: so there is some anger that the state provides offenders with separate education and opportunities to prepare for this exam.
Father Jeong Min-ha, of the Archdiocese of Seoul's correctional ministry committee, worked with Seoul Southern Correctional Institution from September 2023 until last year.
He acknowledges these criticisms.
"Studying gives them a sense of achievement and time to look seriously at their own lives. That's why I think it matters. I think that is the most important part of rehabilitation."
Of course, there is no guarantee.
Park recalls a student who had done well at the school but later returned to prison.
"He was doing well when he left, but in the end he came back. So something went wrong. I'd hoped he would carry on with what he'd been doing here, but he couldn't. That's disappointing."
According to the justice ministry's 2026 corrections statistical yearbook, 35.5% of prisoners aged under 20 who were released in 2021 were imprisoned again within three years. That was about 1.7 times the overall rate of 21.2%, and the highest of any age group.
But Park hopes the students will continue learning after they leave prison. "We don't know what the outcome will be," he says.
"They say the way to clear a glass of dirty water is to keep pouring clean water into it, rather than trying to remove each bit of dirt. I hope they fill their minds with good things, learn to use their energy and intellect in the right way, and put that learning into practice at the right time and place."
Additional reporting by Hosu Lee.

noticias.titulo: Kidnap, child marriage and poverty: Why millions of Nigerian children can't go to school
noticias.resumen: BBC World Service launches programme in Hausa for out-of-school children in West Africa.
noticias.texto:
Kidnap, child marriage and poverty: Why millions of Nigerian children can't go to school
- Published
As she pounds millet, 15-year-old Hadiza sings the English alphabet. It is a reminder of something that she desperately misses - going to school.
"Sometimes I write on the ground to practise and see if I'm still writing correctly," she says.
One night, about two years ago, a group of armed men raided her village.
"They scared our cattle away and abducted a girl. We had to run away. We walked barefoot all the way here," she says.
Since then she has lived in a displaced persons camp in Goronyo, a few kilometres from her home. For a short while she went to school here, but soon met a young man and, at the age of 13, stopped going to classes and got married.
"It's tradition here that once a girl is married, her education ends," she explains.
Now she lives with her in-laws and helps look after the home.
Although Nigerian law prohibits marriage under the age of 18, it is not always enforced.
Hadiza is one of nearly 19 million children in Nigeria who are missing out on an education, according to estimates shared by Unesco in 2024. That's about one in four of the country's school-age children.
Against this backdrop, the BBC World Service has launched Dars Hausa, an educational programme in the main language spoken in northern Nigeria, as well as neighbouring Niger, Cameroon and elsewhere in West Africa.
It brings English, maths and science lessons to children across West Africa, via social media, local television partnerships and radio. Many people in the region get their news from the radio and nearly half of households in Nigeria have one, according to the charity Save the Children.
Dars means "lesson" in Pashto and Dari, and it was first launched in those languages in 2023 for Afghan children barred from attending school. An Arabic version followed in February 2025.
The reasons why so many Nigerian children are out of school are numerous and complex. Like Hadiza, 12-year-old Rukayya also lives in the displacement camp in Goronyo.
"It pains me to see other children studying and going to school while I cannot," she says.
As the eldest child, each day Rukayya goes out to gather firewood to sell and to beg so that her younger siblings can have something to eat.
"If my father was alive, I wouldn't have to go out and beg," she explains, saying some people mock her "but it doesn't stop me because it is our only way to survive."
Bandits killed her father about a year ago in front of her, she says, and her family fled from their home to the camp.
She and Hadiza are among 670,000 people in north-west and central Nigeria who have been forced from their homes by armed robbery and kidnappings, according to the International Organization for Migration.
- Three Girls: Lessons in Limbo features the stories of Hadiza and Rukayya - you can watch the full film on YouTube, external
Some attacks have been carried out by militant Islamist groups, but the majority in this region are by criminal gangs, known in Nigeria as bandits, who steal, kill and kidnap.
The school that Hadiza once attended in Goronyo is the only one serving children in the camp and typically has about 50 students in each class.
One of the teachers, Kamilu Sulaiman Jakada, says that even though lessons are free, only a tiny portion of the children attend, and even then sporadically, because parents tell him that "it is the children that are the breadwinners" and they need to earn money to eat.
He says the school does not have enough teachers or classrooms, explaining that funding is inconsistent and often comes from individuals or organisations rather than the government.
The other challenge is the bandits. A gang once came to the school on motorbikes, shooting in the air, he says, and although no-one was hurt, many parents were scared and withdrew their children. That has been parents' reaction to attacks in some other parts of the country too.
Every Nigerian child is meant to get nine years of free, compulsory education - six in primary and three in secondary school. Responsibility is shared between federal, state and local governments.
But many schools are facing shortages and poorer families who cannot afford private education can struggle to pay for uniforms, books and transport.
The crisis has built up over decades, with successive governments struggling to address chronic underfunding and poor oversight of resources.
In addition, many children in the traditional Almajiri system, which provides Islamic education, are not taught subjects such as maths and science, and are considered by Unicef to be out of school.
Minister of State for Education Prof Suwaiba Sa'id believes the number of children out of school is lower than has been reported, but admits that with Nigeria's growing population "the proper investment, the proper oversight, has not been doneâ¦ I will not mention the names, but we know of two states that did not recruit a single teacher for eight years".
She says that education is the government's "number-one priority" and initiatives such as Lumina are designed to help address "decades of neglect". Lumina aims to support one million girls by 2030, providing an accelerated learning programme for older girls who have missed years of formal education.
She also says that "the government is doing everything possible" to deal with bandits and that "we have seen children that should be at school but are engaged in this banditry".
In the meantime, it is children like Hadiza and Rukayya that the BBC World Service Dars Hausa programmes aim to help. Hadiza says she still has a dream to one day become a doctor "to help my fellow women".
Dars Hausa will air on BBC News Hausa radio on Sundays at 06:45 West Africa Time, with a repeat at 20:45. The programme will also be available via BBC News Hausa's digital platforms, including YouTube, Facebook, X and Instagram.
