noticias.titulo: EU agrees to resurrect cooperation deal with Syria
noticias.resumen: Decision aims to bolster bloc's ties with Damascus following the collapse of Assad's government in December 2024.
noticias.texto:
EU agrees to resurrect cooperation deal with Syria
Decision aims to bolster the bloc’s ties with Damascus following the Assad government’s collapse in December 2024.
European Union foreign ministers have agreed to revive a nearly 20-year-old cooperation deal with Syria, as the bloc presses to strengthen ties with the war-scarred country.
“Syria needs investment and a successful transition,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Monday.
“The aim is to give Europe and Syria a framework for trade, political dialogue and closer cooperation as soon as possible.”
The EU-Syria association agreement was first made in 2008 under then-President Bashar al-Assad, but it was never fully signed by either side, owing to concerns over the Assad government’s human rights record.
Kallas said EU foreign ministers meeting in Brussels had “supported moving ahead” with that deal and launching talks for an updated one.
A discussion paper prepared by the bloc’s diplomatic service ahead of the meeting outlined one of Brussels’ most ambitious efforts yet to normalise ties with Syria, less than two years after Assad’s fall.
Kallas said diplomats would now work through the technical and legal details to finalise the agreement, which would create a framework for free trade, political dialogue and broader cooperation between Brussels and Damascus.
“Everybody said that we need to engage with Syria because if we don’t engage, then this vacuum will be filled by other players,” Kallas said.
Kallas said the EU would set out new conditions for Syria to secure an updated deal.
“We should have clear conditionality regarding human rights,” she said.
“We should have also the nonrecognition of occupied Ukrainian, Georgian territories that they have recognised under Assad’s regime.”
The move is the latest in the 27-nation bloc’s efforts to bolster ties with Damascus and its new leader, President Ahmed al-Sharaa.
The EU in 2025 removed its crushing sanctions on Syria’s economy in a bid to help its recovery after almost 14 years of civil war.
At the start of 2026, Brussels announced a two-year funding package worth 620 million euros ($680m) for the country.
The 53-year-long rule of the Assad family ended on December 8, 2024, after an 11-day offensive that took Syria and the world by surprise.
It also halted a lengthy civil war that left lasting scars on the country and saw some 6.8 million Syrians, about one-third of the population, flee abroad.
More than one million Syrian refugees have already returned home since Assad’s fall, while millions more among the diaspora weigh the decision to do the same and rebuild their lives in their homeland.

noticias.titulo: US Pentagon rejects allegations linking deputy to a Goldman Sachs banker
noticias.resumen: Pentagon defends Steve Feinberg, amid claims in Bloomberg he encouraged defence contractors to use a specific banker.
noticias.texto:
US Pentagon rejects allegations linking deputy to a Goldman Sachs banker
The Department of Defense has defended Steve Feinberg amid claims that he encouraged defence contractors to use a specific banker.
The Pentagon has denied reports that Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg pushed defence contractors to work with a specific Goldman Sachs banker with whom he had longstanding ties.
In a statement sent to Al Jazeera on Monday, the Pentagon said the allegations were “baseless”.
“Any claim that the Deputy directed companies to use Goldman Sachs is categorically false. He worked with financial firms across the industry throughout his entire career,” Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in the statement.
“He has no favorites, and neither does the Department of War.”
The publication Bloomberg first reported the allegations, citing anonymous sources familiar with the matter.
According to Bloomberg’s report, Feinberg guided defence contractors like Lockheed Martin and RTX towards working with Goldman Sachs banker Jim Donovan during their negotiations with the Pentagon.
Donovan and Feinberg reportedly knew each other. Bloomberg said Donovan has previously worked for the investment firm Feinberg co-founded, Cerberus Capital Management, which claims to oversee $70bn in assets.
Bloomberg’s report has raised concerns about a conflict of interest during the lucrative Pentagon negotiations.
Defence contracts are often million, if not billion, dollar deals. Guiding a company that is competing for a contract to work with a specific banker could be seen as a way of rigging the negotiations.
It would also put the banker in line to potentially receive large commissions from the contracts in question.
According to Bloomberg, both RTX and Lockheed Martin hired Donovan after Feinberg’s suggestion.
The Pentagon, however, has accused Bloomberg of seeking to lend credibility to unsubstantiated allegations.
“Despite the Department’s categorical denial, Bloomberg appears more interested in advancing a baseless smear than establishing the facts. Your sources are playing you, and Bloomberg should know better,” Deputy Pentagon Press Secretary Jacob Bliss told Al Jazeera.
“The Deputy is a man of honor and integrity. Unfortunately, some would rather see him fail than succeed.”
Feinberg was nominated by President Donald Trump for his position in one of the Pentagon’s top posts.
The Senate confirmed him in a vote of 59 to 40, and he was sworn in as the 36th deputy defense secretary on March 17, 2025, according to the Pentagon.
Lockheed Martin and RTX, both aerospace and defence companies, have longstanding ties to the Pentagon.
In August, for instance, the Department of Defense announced a multibillion-dollar deal with Lockheed Martin and another defence giant Northrop Grumman to boost production of parts for the Patriot PAC-3 and THAAD missile interceptor systems.
According to Bloomberg’s reporting, Donovan, the banker, was a part of several deals in recent months involving Lockheed Martin and RTX.
They include a $59bn contract with Lockheed Martin for Patriot missiles and two missile contracts worth approximately $45bn with RTX.
It is unclear who the anonymous sources for Bloomberg’s story might be.
Under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon has opened multiple investigations into leaks of sensitive information and taken steps to limit journalists’ access to military officials and other Pentagon resources.

noticias.titulo: Germany thrash Netherlands to book Nations League quarterfinal spot
noticias.resumen: Jurgen Klopp's side outclasses the Dutch 5-0 in Berlin to secure top spot in UEFA Nations League Group A2.
noticias.texto:
Germany thrash Netherlands to book Nations League quarterfinal spot
Jurgen Klopp’s side outclasses the Dutch 5-0 in Berlin to secure the top spot in UEFA Nations League Group A2.
An impressive Germany swept aside off-colour Netherlands 5-0 in Berlin to pip the Dutch to first place in UEFA Nations League Group A2.
Germany needed a win to stand a chance of reaching the quarterfinals, starting the night in third place behind Greece, who had won 1-0 in Germany in September, by virtue of their head-to-head record.
Jurgen Klopp’s side produced a fine attacking display to inflict the heaviest defeat on the Dutch in 67 years, as Xavi Hernandez’s side looked very ragged as they shipped four goals in 17 second-half minutes.
Greece’s win over Serbia left the top three sides level on 11 points, but Germany took the top spot on head-to-head while the Dutch finished second, qualifying for the last eight on goal difference thanks largely to their 7-0 win over Greece on Friday.
After a quiet opening 20 minutes, Kai Havertz headed straight at keeper Bart Verbruggen from a Joshua Kimmich free-kick, while Donyell Malen headed a Cody Gakpo cross from the left of the area over the bar from close range soon after.
Berlin-born Derry Scherhant fired a half-volley against the outside of the Dutch post on 32 minutes after collecting a cross from the right byline, but it turned out to be a range-finder as Scherhant scored his first international goal from a similar position on 44 minutes. After cutting in from the left of the area and working space, he flashed an unstoppable shot past Verbruggen and into the far top corner.
Scherhant almost grabbed his second a minute after the interval as he jinked and bundled his way through on goal on the left of the area only to lash a left-footed effort over the bar with only Verbruggen to beat.
Denzel Dumfries headed over the bar at the other end after running onto a bouncing cross at the back post after ghosting past Scherhant on 48 minutes. Meanwhile, the lively Brajan Gruda came close to a spectacular second at the other end after some neat control and cutting in from the right before flashing a shot past the upright from the edge of the Dutch box.
Soon after, Gakpo tested ter Stegen with a low strike from outside the box, but Germany made him pay as Florian Wirtz doubled the lead with a stunning strike into the top corner from the edge of the D with his left foot on the hour.
Nico Schlotterbeck glanced home a header from Gruda’s curling free-kick from the left within five minutes to make it 3-0, and the fourth arrived soon after as Gruda was allowed to glide into the area on the right and get to the byline before dinking the ball back into the middle for the unmarked Wirtz to lash home his second goal with a volley off the underside of the bar.
Gruda nearly added a goal to his two assists as his rising shot was stopped by Verbruggen after another silky run, but the 22-year-old eventually marked his second cap with his second international goal on 77 minutes when he fired home the rebound after Scherhant’s shot came back off the inside of the post.
It led to Verbruggen calling an impromptu huddle outside his area as the visitors sought to end their misery, and they saw the game out without further alarm.
Germany will be seeded in Friday’s draw for the last eight, which will be contested over two legs in March.

noticias.titulo: European-made pesticides named in 1,605 poisoning reports in Brazil last year
noticias.resumen: About a third of cases involved chemicals banned for use on EU farms, according to investigation by Unearthed and Public Eye Pesticides sold by European chemical companies were named in more than 1,600 poisoning reports in Brazil last year, an investigation has found. About a third of the cases involved chemicals banned from use on farms in the EU because of the risks they pose to people and the environment. But European companies are not banned from manufacturing these chemicals, as long as they export them overseas to countries where they are legally allowed to be used. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Pesticides sold by European chemical companies were named in more than 1,600 poisoning reports in Brazil last year, an investigation has found.
About a third of the cases involved chemicals banned from use on farms in the EU because of the risks they pose to people and the environment. But European companies are not banned from manufacturing these chemicals, as long as they export them overseas to countries where they are legally allowed to be used.
Analysis of Brazilian health ministry data by Unearthed and Public Eye in a report published on Tuesday found that of 2,857 poisoning reports that named an identifiable agricultural product, 1,605 named brands sold by European pesticide companies.
Farm workers in Brazil have described their flesh rotting, skin burning, difficulty breathing and vomiting after using the chemicals at work, according to the report. A small number have died accidentally or killed themselves by drinking the pesticides.
Under Brazilian law, reports must be submitted by healthcare professionals to Brazil’s national disease notification system in all suspected pesticide poisoning cases. These reports can be marked “confirmed” poisoning or “exposure” only by the doctor or nurse who saw the patient.
Clinicians sometimes record cases as exposure when they lack the training or support to confirm a diagnosis, but are presented with a patient who says they have been exposed to pesticides or present symptoms of pesticide poisoning. Laboratory confirmation is rare, so recording a diagnosis of “confirmed” poisoning usually depends on clinical judgment.
Experts say clinicians can be reluctant to confirm cases because of a lack of training or support. A brand being named in a poisoning report is not proof that it caused poisoning or death.
“The insufficient training of healthcare professionals to recognise and manage these cases is a major limiting factor,” said Vanda Garibotti, a public health biologist at the State Centre for Health Surveillance in Rio Grande do Sul, southern Brazil.
High staff turnover and a lack of institutional support meant poisoning cases were rarely confirmed through laboratory tests and often relied on clinical judgment, Garibotti added.
In more than 6,700 medical reports involving agricultural pesticides last year, 2,857 named an identifiable product. Of those, 1,420 were classified as confirmed poisonings. A further 1,108 were classified as exposures; for the remainder the classification was unknown or other diagnoses.
Some of the products are made in Britain. Reglone is the most frequently cited UK-made weedkiller. It contains diquat, a chemical that was banned in the UK in 2020 after experts concluded it posed a high risk to people living near fields where it was sprayed. Diquat is also found in other pesticides.
Despite the usage ban, Reglone is still manufactured by the Swiss-headquartered pesticides company Syngenta at its factory in Huddersfield for export to countries with more permissive regulations, including Brazil.
Nelson Castoldi died last year after accidentally ingesting Reglone on his family farm in Rio Grande do Sul. To save money, his family had bought the weedkiller in bulk, decanting a single litre into an empty cola bottle to avoid hauling a heavy 20-litre canister into the fields.
Working under the scorching sun, Castoldi mistook the black chemical for a soft drink and took a sip. Though he spat it out immediately, the chemical caused his kidneys to fail before attacking his lungs. He died two days later.
“We fell apart,” Ivan Castoldi said of his father’s death. “Four months after our father passed away, our mother also passed away. She cried day and night. She became depressive and had a stroke. She was left alone.
“That poison, Reglone, should be banned in Brazil,” he added. “Not because of what happened to us, but because of its toxicity.”
The Brazilian health ministry recorded 75 cases involving diquat last year, compared with 36 over the five years from 2018 to 2022.
The investigation found Reglone was specifically named in 44 reports, including four deaths. Of those cases, 26 were classified as confirmed poisonings and the rest were classified as exposure, unknown, or adverse reaction.
Dormex, a pesticide manufactured in Germany by Alzchem and distributed in Brazil by the German chemical company BASF, is another product workers said injured them or made them ill.
Sidnei Souza de Oliveira, 49, suffered a severe injury after a jug of Dormex spilled on his leg while he was filling a sprayer. The handle broke as he was transferring the chemical into the tank. At first, his leg turned red, and he continued spraying.
He carried on working for four days before going to hospital. “After 15 days, my leg was black. Chunks of flesh were falling off,” Oliveira said. A doctor said the injury was serious and had to remove dead tissue to stop it spreading towards the bone.
Oliveira said the protective trousers supplied by his employer were thin and allowed the chemical to seep through. He said he had been afraid of losing his job if he stayed away from work for too long.
Dormex contains cyanamide, which was banned from use in the EU in 2008 because of concerns about its effects on human health, particularly among farm workers spraying the chemical. Analysis shows the Brazilian health ministry database recorded 17 confirmed poisonings involving Dormex last year.
Finale, a BASF product identified in the investigation, contains glufosinate, which was banned in the EU in 2018. Roundup – a glyphosate-based weedkiller manufactured by the German chemical company Bayer – was frequently cited in Brazilian poisoning reports, including 12 deaths.
Across all the poisoning reports identified by the investigation as involving products sold by European companies, there were 32 reported deaths. Of these cases, 31 were classified as confirmed poisonings, and 26 were recorded as suicides.
Syngenta products were cited 425 times in the poisoning reports, and BASF 179 times. The company figures are not mutually exclusive: some poisoning reports named products sold by more than one manufacturer.
Nina Schrank, a senior campaigner at Greenpeace UK, said the findings were a “deadly double standard”.
“If a pesticide is too dangerous to use in Britain, it should be too dangerous to export. Ministers must stop allowing Britain to be part of a production line for toxic chemicals that are putting lives at risk overseas.”
The EU’s pesticide approval system requires chemicals to meet strict standards for human and animal health and the environment. Diquat has been banned on EU and UK farms since 2019 and 2020 respectively, after experts concluded it posed a high risk to workers, people living nearby and birds. Cyanamide was withdrawn after an assessment found exposure among agricultural operators could exceed safe levels. Glufosinate, meanwhile, is classified in the EU as toxic to reproduction, meaning it can harm fertility or the development of unborn children.
Suicide prevention is also a factor. A 2020 study found national bans on highly hazardous pesticides could be a cost-effective intervention for reducing the number of people who kill themselves in countries with a high burden of suicides attributable to pesticides.
A Syngenta spokesperson said almost half the Brazilian cases attributed to the company were not classified as confirmed poisonings, adding: “Public Eye and Unearthed are aware of this but have explicitly chosen to disregard the dataset’s final classification.” The company accused the investigation of disregarding the dataset’s final classifications and identified “numerous other inconsistencies” that it said raised “serious concerns” that the evidence was “being selectively interpreted to support a predetermined conclusion”.
“There are real people behind these statistics. Every genuine case of poisoning matters, and every family affected deserves our concern,” the spokesperson added.
Syngenta said Brazil had its own “robust regulatory system” and that products banned in Europe could still be independently assessed and legally registered in the country, citing differences in crops, growing conditions and pest pressures. It said it trained 95,000 people in Brazil in the safe use of its products in 2025, including through free online courses.
Bayer said its products were safe when used according to label instructions, citing what it described as rigorous testing and assessments by global health authorities. The company said it took pesticide poisoning seriously but questioned the reliability of the data, arguing that products and circumstances of exposure had not been independently verified, some chemicals may have been incorrectly identified and symptoms such as headaches and skin irritation could have other causes.
It said “Roundup” was “widely used as a generic term” that could refer to weedkillers made by other manufacturers or counterfeit products.
The company said it provided training on the safe handling and use of pesticides, including protective equipment, and that its programmes reached more than 4 million people globally in 2025. It also argued that a pesticide being banned in the EU did not necessarily mean it was unsafe, saying other countries had robust regulatory systems that took account of local agricultural conditions.
It added: “While the data presented helps to provide information on broad trends of exposure, the data has limitations and warrants caution when drawing conclusions, particularly when looking at individual cases.”
BASF said it was deeply concerned by reports of poisoning that might be linked to its products, adding that it took all such incidents seriously.
A spokesperson said publicly available information suggested some incidents might have involved the intentional ingestion of crop protection products, describing such acts as “deliberate misuse” of products intended exclusively for agricultural use.
BASF said it had global and local procedures to assess and investigate incidents potentially involving its products, and worked with authorities and experts where appropriate to understand cases and identify ways to prevent similar incidents. It said it invested in education and training to promote the safe handling and use of its products, with initiatives in Brazil reaching more than 14,475 participants in 2025.
The company said it was confident in the safety of its products when used in accordance with label instructions and applicable regulatory standards.
It added that Brazilian law required crop protection products to be handled and applied only by authorised and properly trained individuals, and said it took its responsibility for ensuring their safe use seriously.

noticias.titulo: Hundreds arrested in anti-Trump protests in Philippines amid anger over Iran war and AI pact

noticias.texto:
Hundreds of people have been arrested in heated demonstrations against Donald Trump in Manila, as authorities braced for more protests ahead of the US president’s arrival in the city for a leaders’ summit.
Organisers claim as many as 10,000 people will join protests against Trump in the Philippine capital on Tuesday, when he will attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit. The crowds are expected to try to walk to the summit site.
Authorities have arrested nearly 300 people in widespread protests in held in the days leading up to the summit, with large parts of the capital closed off and tight security in place.
Some burned effigies of Trump and faced off with police officers armed with batons and shields. Slogans on placards called the American leader the world’s “number one terrorist” in protests held on Monday.
Demonstrators angry at the cost-of-living and energy shock caused by the Iran war, and the new US-led Pax Silica initiative on AI and critical minerals, tried to reach the summit at the Philippine International Convention Center on Monday, but were blocked by police.
Pax Silica has sparked tensions in the Philippines over plans to build a tech hub outside Manila that critics say will affect water and energy supplies, and displace members of the Ayta Indigenous community.
Large sections of central Manila were closed to the public as part of the security cordon, and public holidays instituted for the Asean summit.
Trump will meet with the leaders of Australia, Japan and India on Tuesday night before heading to Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday. There he will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and hold trilateral talks with China’s president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.
The backlash against Trump follows the ouster of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, and allegations members of the US administration, including the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, knew about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump’s delegation was expected to include businessman Elon Musk.
Protest leader Renato Reyes blamed the arrests in Manila on the heavy handed response of the government on the president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr., calling Monday the largest single day of police arrests since Marcos came to office in 2022.
“It is really crazy that the Philippine government is rolling out the red carpet for someone who has been so flatly rejected by the American people,” Reyes said.
“Trump started a war that devastated the global economy and pushed oil prices in the Philippines to historic highs. It has caused untold suffering on the Filipino people.
“So yes, Trump will have to pay for his crimes and he will have to be answerable, not just to the American people, but to the people of the world.”
The Philippine national police said some officers were injured during confrontations with demonstrators opposed to the summit, including when objects were allegedly thrown at officers.
Pax Silica will include a technology hub planned at New Clark City in Tarlac, about 120km from Manila.
Intended to bolster western stocks of AI technology and reduce “excessive dependencies” on single source supply chains, including from China, Pax Silica will provide chips and critical minerals to 25 participating signatory governments.
Amnesty Philippines said demonstrations should not be forcibly or violently dispersed.
“Reports of arrests during the protests demand immediate scrutiny,” director Ritz Lee Santos III said.
“Authorities must explain the specific grounds for each arrest and any continued detention. Anyone detained solely for peacefully exercising their rights must be released immediately.”

noticias.titulo: Rio Tinto agrees to pay US$250m to begin repairing ‘devastation’ left by Panguna mine
noticias.resumen: Community leader says fund gives chance to find solutions to ‘huge problems we have been living with since the days of the mine’s operation’ Anglo-Australian miner Rio Tinto has agreed to pay a quarter-of-a-billion dollars to begin the clean-up of the toxic Panguna mine site it abandoned more than three decades ago. Panguna, once one of the world’s most profitable gold and copper mines, was shuttered in 1989 after violent protests over environmental damage and the inequitable division of the mine’s profits sparked a decade-long civil war on the Papua New Guinean island of Bougainville. Continu
noticias.texto:
Anglo-Australian miner Rio Tinto has agreed to pay a quarter-of-a-billion dollars to begin the clean-up of the toxic Panguna mine site it abandoned more than three decades ago.
Panguna, once one of the world’s most profitable gold and copper mines, was shuttered in 1989 after violent protests over environmental damage and the inequitable division of the mine’s profits sparked a decade-long civil war on the Papua New Guinean island of Bougainville.
But the sprawling mine pit, once a mountain, remains a scar in the middle of the island, with vast pillars of rubble at risk of collapse, and polluted rivers running bright blue with toxins.
Rio Tinto was forced from the island and has never returned, but in recent years has been part of a detailed consultation process with landowners and government. It has now agreed to voluntarily contribute US$250m (A$370m) towards the remediation of the mine site.
Theonila Roka Matbob, a former cabinet minister in Bougainville’s autonomous government and Panguna community leader, said the fund was a vital contribution towards repairing the “devastation left by the Panguna mine”.
“We have a lot of work still ahead of us, but the establishment of this fund gives us the chance to find solutions to the huge problems we have been living with since the days of the mine’s operation.
“No amount of money will restore the damage caused to the environment in Panguna, but this sets a foundation for us to invest in addressing the environmental issues and invest in our children’s futures as well.”
Roka Matbob said the most fundamental remediation was to improve “accessibility” for the people living around Panguna – “accessibility to clean drinking water that is safe and secure … and infrastructure, in bridges that makes people’s access to trade, to school, to health[care], much easier. This is one critical area that immediately needs attention.”
The president of Bougainville, Ishmael Toroama, seeking to become the world’s newest head of state at the forefront of a long-running independence movement on the island, said the money would make a “meaningful difference” to villages and communities that had suffered from the impacts of the mine’s pollution.
“This work will deliver benefits not only for people today, but for future generations. Continued engagement with our communities will be essential to ensuring the work responds to local priorities and delivers lasting outcomes.”
The Rio commitment has emerged from the Panguna Mine Legacy Impact Assessment consultation process, which was initiated in response to a human rights complaint brought by the Australian-based Human Rights Law Centre, with Roka Matbob as the lead complainant.
Keren Adams, the HRLC’s legal director, said establishing the fund had taken years of work.
“It is a testament to the courage and persistence of community leaders, and the willingness of all parties to engage in difficult but constructive dialogue,” she said.
“The significant funding contributed by Rio Tinto creates a real opportunity to now address an environmental disaster that has remained unresolved for decades.”
Mark Davies, Rio Tinto’s chief safety and technical officer, said the establishment of the fund was an “important milestone … intended to support the transition from the assessment to practical remedy implementation”.
“Community engagement is an important next step to identify priorities and we remain committed to working with communities to shape the activities supported by the fund.”
The quarter-of-a-billion dollars will not be sufficient to entirely remediate the mine site, but it is being seen as a major step towards rehabilitation.
The funding commitment for Panguna comes at an acutely sensitive time for the restive Bougainville island.
The mine has become inextricably linked with the Bougainville’s political future: restarting operations at Panguna – believed to still hold at least $60bn in unrealised reserves – is seen by many, including the president, as the fundamental financial basis for the island’s independent future. Indian miner Lloyds has been granted a 25-year large-scale mining lease, but any future mining is years from starting.
Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly $2bn from Panguna over 17 years of operation from 1972. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands were destroyed by it.
Disaffected landowners ran a sabotage campaign that forced Panguna’s closure in 1989. The PNG government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war – known as “the crisis” – that ran for a decade. Between 15,000 and 20,000 people were killed, roughly 10% of the island’s population.
A recent environmental impact assessment found the abandoned mine remains an acute threat to people’s lives, including from landslides, levee collapses and floods. Untouched, the river delta will stay polluted for a century.
The future of Bougainville’s independence campaign is now before the PNG parliament, which will decide whether or not to recognise a UN-backed independence referendum held on the island in 2019, in which 97.7% of voters were in favour of Bougainville seceding and becoming an independent country.
The PNG parliament, which heard lengthy and impassioned debate over Bougainville last month, appears almost certain to vote against recognising the referendum result.
But Toroama, who has staked his presidency on achieving political independence, has said, regardless of the parliament’s decision, Bougainville will enter a period of “self-government” from September next year, before seceding, breaking away from PNG as a fully fledged independent nation, by 2030.

noticias.titulo: ‘Disgusted by it’: body of Melbourne Cup race horse found dumped in Sydney skip bin
noticias.resumen: So You Are placed eighth in race just two weeks ago and was put down after a severe bout of colic Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast The body of a horse that placed eighth in Australia’s Melbourne Cup two weeks ago and recently fell ill has been found dumped in skip bin in Sydney. The horse So You Are, a five-year-old gelding, was put down after it suffered from a severe bout from colic and was taken to hospital on Monday for surgery. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The body of a horse that placed eighth in Australia’s Melbourne Cup two weeks ago and recently fell ill has been found dumped in skip bin in Sydney.
The horse So You Are, a five-year-old gelding, was put down after it suffered from a severe bout from colic and was taken to hospital on Monday for surgery.
The same day, Gregg Jowett posted to his personal social media account a video that showed a dead horse inside a skip bin in Sydney. Guardian Australia has chosen not to publish the video.
“I’m at the tip. It’s a fucking horse. They tipped a horse in the fucking bin at the tip,” he can be heard saying in the video.
“[I’m] quite shocked about that; that’s not normal. Please let me know if I’m wrong, but that’s not normal.”
Jowett later told Guardian Australia he didn’t know when he found the horse that it was So You Are, or a horse that had competed in Australia’s most famous race, the Melbourne Cup.
“I’m just disgusted by it,” he said.
The horse’s trainer, Bjorn Baker, said the handling of So You Are’s remains had compounded an already devastating loss.
“Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the apparent handling of So You Are’s remains,” he said in a statement.
“He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death.
“I understand the hospital facility REC Equine Specialists are investigating the circumstances, and I expect a full explanation of what occurred.
“My thoughts remain with [So You Are breeders] the Ramsey family, and with all my staff, for whom this has compounded an already devastating loss.”
Dr Jonathan Lumsden, the managing partner of REC Equine Specialists, which treated So You Are after he was brought to the service with colic, apologised “unreservedly for the distress caused by footage shared on social media today”.
“Despite the best efforts of our veterinary team, he could not be saved and was humanely euthanised under anaesthesia,” Lumsden said.
“After his death, So You Are was collected by our contracted provider and taken to a licensed landfill. He should have been promptly and respectfully buried.
“What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone who cared for him. We are deeply sorry.
“So You Are was in our care. We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that. We should have known exactly how horses were handled after leaving our hospital, and we did not. That process is not good enough, and it must change.
“We have spoken with So You Are’s owners and trainer to apologise personally,” he said. “We are working with our disposal provider and the facility operators, together with Racing NSW, to establish how this happened and to put in processes to ensure it never happens again.”
Lumsden said the service had, effective immediately, stopped using the contract provider and was undertaking a review of how other providers care for horses after death.
“Out of respect for So You Are and those who loved him, we ask that the footage not be shared further,” Lumsden said.
David Harris, the minister for gaming and racing, said Racing NSW had launched an investigation into the incident.
“This is a concerning incident, the racing legislative framework and Racing NSW as the sport’s controlling body has measures in place to safeguard racing integrity and animal welfare,” he said.
Georgie Purcell, the Animal Justice party MP for northern Victoria,
 
said the incident should “force serious questions the industry’s so-called duty of care”.
“The racing industry breeds these horses and profits for them but fails the most basic obligation to treat them with dignity after death,” she said.

noticias.titulo: Woman whose baby died after free birth didn’t know she was pregnant with twins, NSW inquest hears

noticias.texto:
A northern rivers mother whose baby died after a free birth did not know she was having twins until she was in labour after having no pregnancy scans, the New South Wales coroner’s court has heard.
The inquest will examine the deaths of four babies born in free births or home births who died in the northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024. It will consider whether the care was reasonable in the circumstances and whether care by an unregistered support worker was reasonable and appropriate before, during and after the birth. Free births are when a person gives birth without a registered health professional present.
Both of the twins died – one was stillborn and most likely died in the womb before he was born, and one died within three hours of birth, the inquest heard. Only Baby D, who was born alive, is included in the inquest – coroner’s courts cannot examine the death of a stillborn baby. It is unclear why Baby D died, but the court heard it was possible the baby died from blood loss after the umbilical cord was cut but not clamped.
The inquest heard on Tuesday that the mother – who cannot be named for legal reasons – had decided to do a “sovereign birth”, where a woman gives birth at home on her own.
The mother had three to four sessions with Sita Tara Kali, a self-described birth keeper, before the birth, according to a statement the mother gave to police that was read to the inquest. She was paid a fee of $4,100.
Kali, who is expected to give evidence at a later date, was involved in the care of two of the four babies included in the inquest. She is not facing criminal charges.
The mother said in the police statement that her sessions with Kali before the birth were “mostly bodywork”. She said: “I didn’t get anything much out of the system in terms of birth preparation, a few books. Nothing of the quality she offered me.” The court heard that Kali had performed “body mapping”, but did not identify that there were two babies.
She said she felt “vibrant” and “healthy” during the pregnancy and the birth was “amazing”.
The mother only realised she was having another baby after giving birth to the first baby.
She said Kali advised them to ring an ambulance immediately, according to the police statement.
Sgt David Greenway told the inquest on Tuesday that when he arrived at the family’s house in 2024, he found one of the newborn twins had died. The other baby was on its way to hospital, he said.
The second twin, referred to as Baby D, did not survive.
Greenway said the parents were in shock and had not known they were expecting twins.
Greenway told the inquest that Kali was present at the house and said to him: “I’m the birth keeper, so I support women that want to free birth.
“I am not medically trained. And there is a big need because a lot of women don’t want to go to the hospital, and they can’t afford midwives. I’m not doing anything illegal. I know my rights,” Greenway recalled her saying.
“When people are choosing to be in their sovereignty, it is up to them what they choose to do,” Kali said, according to Greenway.
Dr Alison Teate, the president of the Australian College of Midwives, told the inquest on Tuesday if there are two twins and one placenta, they are at a higher risk category than if there are two placentas.
“The level of surveillance goes up significantly. It would be appointments every fortnight, from 20 weeks,” she said.
The inquest heard the neonatal expert Prof Nicholas Evans believed both twins would probably have survived if the pregnancy had been managed conventionally.
In the police statement, the mother said: “Our decision to not systemize our birth was very prominent. We decided to not have scans and try to birth as holistically and spiritually as possible. Which would mean that we would have a home birth out of the system with a doula who is incredibly experienced.”
The inquest continues.

noticias.titulo: David Jones: what went wrong and what happens next? Five takeaways from first creditors meeting
noticias.resumen: Upmarket retailer, which recorded a net loss of $228m last financial year, has total debt over $400m including $11m owed to staff Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Upmarket retailer David Jones owed hundreds of millions of dollars when it collapsed into administration, after accelerating financial losses and reputational damage threatened its ability to stock shelves for Christmas. noticias.texto:
Upmarket retailer David Jones owed hundreds of millions of dollars when it collapsed into administration, after accelerating financial losses and reputational damage threatened its ability to stock shelves for Christmas.
About 500 creditors attended its first meeting on Tuesday, where administrators McGrathNicol started to break down who is owed what, when those left out of pocket will know where they stand, and what ultimately went wrong.
Here are five things we learned.
How much is owed?
David Jones collapsed early this month owing in excess of $400m to an assortment of creditors, including $180m of debts to trade creditors, mainly consisting of the brands that stocked its shelves.
There are also outstanding employee entitlements, such as annual and long service leave, worth about $11m, and about $33m in unredeemed gift cards, which the retailer is still accepting.
The rest is owed to large secured creditors, led by the retailer’s main financier, Hilco, which has a controlling hand over the current process and even has its own representatives in the 19 stores marked for closure.
Taken together, the debts are well over $400m, but that total is almost certain to climb as landlords tally up their losses.
On top of unpaid rent up to the appointment of administrators, shopping centre owners will also claim for broken leases after the chain’s receivers moved to close half of its 38-store network.
How much will creditors get back?
What, if any, money suppliers get back hinges on whether a buyer steps in and how much they are willing to pay, or whether the chain ends up liquidated, as well as how much cash David Jones can bring in through the crucial Christmas trading period.
Because product suppliers sit near the bottom of the creditor priority list, they won’t receive any money until secured lenders and employees are paid out.
Given the size of the outstanding debts, and poor financial state of the department chain, many suppliers are bracing for a near total loss of outstanding amounts.
Shaun Fraser, a founding partner at McGrathNicol, told creditors there were “too many variables” to indicate how much, if any, suppliers would receive.
“We haven’t yet got to a point where we’re engaged enough with bidders to have a sense of what value might be there,” Fraser said.
“We haven’t reached a point in the sale process where people are talking value or price.”
How are creditors feeling?
Out of pocket suppliers are particularly frustrated, though the modern practice of holding meetings online kept any real anger contained behind muted microphones.
There were questions over whether there had been preferential treatment to some suppliers, and if the retailer had been trading insolvent before the appointment of administrators.
McGrathNicol said it would investigate when the company might have been insolvent, and if preferential payments were made.
One brand representative said they had also repeatedly asked for stock lists and weekly sales figures without response.
What went wrong?
The administrators provided updated financials at the meeting that showed the poor state of affairs at David Jones.
The 188-year-old retailer recorded a net loss of $228m in 2025-26, before losing a further $69m in the first four months of the new financial year leading up to the administration.
Creditors were told that the funding pressures it was facing, coupled with reputational damage, was affecting its ability to get stock for the Christmas trading period.
David Jones ultimately got tipped into administration when negotiations with its main landlord, Westfield owner Scentre Group, broke down.
The retailer’s private equity owner, Anchorage Capital, wanted to radically reduce store numbers – something that is now happening during receivership – to rid the network of underperforming suburban stores.
The directors of David Jones listed several causes of the retailer’s problems, including everything from cost-of-living pressures and soft luxury demand to fierce online competition.
Fraser said there was also “clearly a business model problem” with the retailer.
What happens next?
Under a dual appointment, receivers FTI Consulting have taken day-to-day control of the business while administrators McGrathNicol hunt for a buyer, having called for “non-binding indicative offers” for the retailer by the end of the month.
That will trigger a process that could see formal bids lodged either late this year or early in 2027, giving some clarity to employees and suppliers ahead of the next creditors’ meeting, due by March.
The road ahead is, however, complicated by the breakdown in relations between Anchorage and the Westfield owner, which is threatening the retailer’s ability to operate at any of its complexes.
The Scentre Group chief executive, Elliott Rusanow, told Guardian Australia the landlord now had a “unique opportunity to facilitate the entry and growth of businesses that are more relevant to customers today and into the future”.
“That is the opportunity we will pursue at each of the 17 destinations with a David Jones store,” Rusanow said.
